questions.q: What distinguishes a true audit trail from a system that merely 'has logs'?
options: An audit trail is specifically built to answer who did what, to which data, when, and with what outcome
An audit trail only records failed actions, never successful ones
An audit trail is any log file regardless of its content
An audit trail is generated exclusively by the database engine
questions.explain: Generic logs (errors, timings) don't necessarily capture attributable identity, specific resources touched, or outcomes — an audit trail is purpose-built to answer those five questions.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a log entry should identify a specific authenticated identity rather than a shared service account?
options: Because a shared account can't be attributed to one specific actor, making 'who' unanswerable during an investigation
Because shared service accounts are always more secure than individual accounts
Because shared accounts are prohibited by every data protection regulation
Because logs cannot technically record service account activity
questions.explain: The 'who' question requires an attributable identity — a shared account that many people could use defeats the purpose of recording who actually performed the action.

questions.q: What does 'tamper-evident' or append-only log storage protect against?
options: Someone editing or deleting log entries after the fact, which would make the audit trail untrustworthy as evidence
Logs growing too large to store cost-effectively
Logs being readable by auditors
Logs being generated in the wrong timestamp format
questions.explain: If log entries can be silently altered or removed, the audit trail can no longer be trusted to reflect what actually happened — tamper-evidence or append-only storage makes such changes detectable or impossible.

questions.q: What tension does this lesson identify between log retention and the retention principles from Lesson 23?
options: Logs need to be kept long enough to support a later investigation, but logs containing personal data also carry over-retention risk like any other personal data
Logs must always be deleted immediately after creation to comply with privacy law
Logs are exempt from all retention considerations because they are not personal data
Logs must be retained permanently with no disposition schedule
questions.explain: Most organizations resolve this by giving logs their own distinct, usually shorter, retention period — long enough to be useful, short enough not to become its own breach liability.

questions.q: In the worked audit log example, what does the OUTCOME field represent?
options: Whether the action succeeded, failed, or was denied
The classification level of the resource accessed
The retention period that applies to the resource
The job title of the actor who performed the action
questions.explain: Outcome is one of the five required elements of a usable audit entry, recording whether the attempted action actually succeeded, failed, or was denied.
